claim: Collagen is a common target in the analysis of ancient organic remains.

claim: Collagen is non-labile relative to many other vertebrate proteins because of its decay resistance.
source: Collagen is also non-labile relative to many other vertebrate proteins because of its decay resistance, partly due to its triple helical quaternary structure and high concentration of thermally stable amino acids (Engel and Bächinger, 2005; Persikov et al., 2005; Sansom et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2012), and it is therefore reasonable to predict that collagen would be more resistant to microbial decay and diagenesis than many other proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on collagen structure and stability.

claim: Collagen's decay resistance is partly due to its triple helical quaternary structure and high concentration of thermally stable amino acids.
source: Collagen is also non-labile relative to many other vertebrate proteins because of its decay resistance, partly due to its triple helical quaternary structure and high concentration of thermally stable amino acids (Engel and Bächinger, 2005; Persikov et al., 2005; Sansom et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2012), and it is therefore reasonable to predict that collagen would be more resistant to microbial decay and diagenesis than many other proteins.

claim: Putative dinosaur soft tissues should contain diagenetically unstable proteins and phospholipids if endogenous.
source: If endogenous, putative dinosaur soft tissues should contain diagenetically unstable proteins and phospholipids (Bada, 1998; Briggs and Summons, 2014), vulnerable to hydrolysis (Eglinton and Logan, 1991; Zuidam and Crommelin, 1995), although the released fatty acid moieties from phospholipids could be stabilized through in situ polymerization into kerogen-like aliphatic structures (Stankiewicz et al., 2000; Gupta et al., 2006a; Gupta et al., 2006b; Gupta et al., 2007a; Gupta et al., 2007b; Gupta et al., 2008; Gupta et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on protein and lipid stability.

claim: Proteins and phospholipids are vulnerable to hydrolysis.

source: At 25°C and neutral pH, peptide bond half-lives from uncatalyzed hydrolysis are too short to allow for Mesozoic peptide preservation, although hydrolysis rates can be decreased through terminal modifications and steric effects on internal bonds (Kahne and Still, 1988; Radzicka and Wolfenden, 1996; Testa and Mayer, 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on peptide bond stability.

claim: Hydrolysis rates of peptide bonds can be decreased through terminal modifications and steric effects on internal bonds.
source: At 25°C and neutral pH, peptide bond half-lives from uncatalyzed hydrolysis are too short to allow for Mesozoic peptide preservation, although hydrolysis rates can be decreased through terminal modifications and steric effects on internal bonds (Kahne and Still, 1988; Radzicka and Wolfenden, 1996; Testa and Mayer, 2003).

source: Such a system might lead not only to the loss of endogenous organics, but also to the influx of subsurface microorganisms that could complicate the detection of any surviving organics, as well as potentially metabolizing them.

claim: The possibility of a microbiome inhabiting fossil bone is very high.
source: The possibility of a microbiome inhabiting fossil bone is very high, especially given that decades of research have revealed the existence of a substantial 'deep biosphere' of living microorganisms actively degrading everything organic from shallow soil organic matter to deeply buried petroleum (Onstott, 2016; Magnabosco et al., 2018), even in million year old permafrost (Amato et al., 2010).

claim: Decades of research have revealed the existence of a substantial 'deep biosphere' of living microorganisms.
source: The possibility of a microbiome inhabiting fossil bone is very high, especially given that decades of research have revealed the existence of a substantial 'deep biosphere' of living microorganisms actively degrading everything organic from shallow soil organic matter to deeply buried petroleum (Onstott, 2016; Magnabosco et al., 2018), even in million year old permafrost (Amato et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Onstott, 2016 and Magnabosco et al., 2018.
