evidence: This is supported by a citation to Amato et al., 2010.

claim: The null hypothesis is that complex biomolecules recovered from dinosaur bones are not original material, more likely representing recent contamination.
source: Since there are theoretical and empirical reasons to believe that dinosaur organics are unlikely to persist for tens of millions of years, and given the potential for contamination, we argue that the null hypothesis is that complex biomolecules (e.g. nucleic acids or proteins) recovered from dinosaur bones are not original material, more likely representing recent contamination.
evidence: This is the authors' proposed null hypothesis based on theoretical and empirical considerations.

claim: Organic material recovered from fossil dinosaur bone will differ in composition from modern vertebrate proteins and tissues, beyond differences expected through normal diagenesis.
source: This hypothesis makes a series of testable predictions: (1) organic material recovered from fossil dinosaur bone will differ in composition (both chemistry and structure) from modern vertebrate proteins and tissues, beyond differences expected through normal diagenesis
evidence: This is a testable prediction derived from the null hypothesis.

claim: Fossils will show evidence for microbial presence.
source: (2) fossils will show evidence for microbial presence (e.g., through nucleic acids or protein)
evidence: This is a testable prediction derived from the null hypothesis.

claim: Fossil bone organic material will show signatures of recent biological activity.
source: (3) fossil bone organic material will show signatures of recent biological activity (e.g. L-amino acid dominance or 14C abundance, which would suggest that the fossils are not isolated from surface processes).
evidence: This is a testable prediction derived from the null hypothesis.

claim: Samples of Late Cretaceous fossil dinosaur bone were obtained from the Dinosaur Park Formation (Late Campanian) in Dinosaur Provincial Park, Alberta, Canada.
source: Samples of Late Cretaceous fossil dinosaur bone, along with associated sediment and soil controls were obtained from the Dinosaur Park Formation (Late Campanian) in Dinosaur Provincial Park, Alberta, Canada (Appendix 1—figures 8–20, Appendix 1—table 2).
evidence: This describes the source of the samples used in the study.

claim: The Dinosaur Park Formation is a well-sampled, alluvial-paralic unit deposited during a transgressive phase of the Western Interior Seaway.
source: The Dinosaur Park Formation is a well-sampled, alluvial-paralic unit deposited during a transgressive phase of the Western Interior Seaway.
evidence: This is geological information about the formation.

claim: A diverse vertebrate fauna has been documented from the Dinosaur Park Formation by more than a century of collection.
source: A diverse vertebrate fauna has been documented from the formation by more than a century of collection (Currie and Koppelhus, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Currie and Koppelhus, 2005.

claim: The bone samples were collected from a monodominant bonebed (BB180) of the centrosaurine Centrosaurus apertus.
source: The bone samples were collected from a monodominant bonebed (BB180) of the centrosaurine Centrosaurus apertus (Ornithischia; Ceratopsidae), located 3 m above the contact with the underlying Oldman Formation (precise location data available at the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology).
evidence: This describes the specific source of the bone samples.

claim: The bonebed is located 3 m above the contact with the underlying Oldman Formation.
source: The bone samples were collected from a monodominant bonebed (BB180) of the centrosaurine Centrosaurus apertus (Ornithischia; Ceratopsidae), located 3 m above the contact with the underlying Oldman Formation (precise location data available at the Royal Tyrrell Museum of Palaeontology).
evidence: This is stratigraphic information about the sample location.

claim: The mudstone-hosted bone-bearing horizon is an aggregation of disarticulated but densely packed bones, with a vertical relief of 15–20 cm.
source: The mudstone-hosted bone-bearing horizon is an aggregation of disarticulated but densely packed bones, with a vertical relief of 15–20 cm.
evidence: This describes the taphonomic characteristics of the bonebed.

claim: The recovered skeletal remains are nearly exclusively from Ceratopsidae, with all diagnostic ceratopsid material assignable to Centrosaurus apertus.
source: Similar to other ceratopsid bonebeds from the same stratigraphic interval (Ryan et al., 2001; Eberth and Getty, 2005), the recovered skeletal remains are nearly exclusively from Ceratopsidae, and with all diagnostic ceratopsid material assignable to Centrosaurus apertus, with the site interpreted as a mass-death assemblage.
evidence: This describes the taxonomic composition of the bonebed.

claim: The site is interpreted as a mass-death assemblage.
source: Similar to other ceratopsid bonebeds from the same stratigraphic interval (Ryan et al., 2001; Eberth and Getty, 2005), the recovered skeletal remains are nearly exclusively from Ceratopsidae, and with all diagnostic ceratopsid material assignable to Centrosaurus apertus, with the site interpreted as a mass-death assemblage.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the taphonomic origin of the bonebed.

claim: Aseptic techniques were implemented during excavation to minimize contamination.
source: At this point, aseptic techniques were then implemented to expose more of the bone in order to determine its size and orientation.
evidence: This describes the methodology used during sample collection.

claim: It is practically impossible to excavate fossils in a truly sterile manner.
source: It is necessary to qualify the usage of the term 'aseptic' in this study. Paleontological field techniques have changed little over the last century, and it is practically impossible to excavate fossils in a truly sterile manner (e.g. the process of matrix removal induces exposure, the wind can carry environmental contaminants onto exposed fossils, etc.).
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of the limitations of field methodology.

claim: Centrosaurus bone vessels were white, Si-dominated with O present, contained holes, and were sometimes infilled with a slightly more prominent C peak internally.
source: VPSEM and EDS of HCl demineralized, freeze-dried dinosaur bones revealed that vessels (and rare fibrous fragments) (Figure 1A,D–E,H–J) were white, Si-dominated with O present, contained holes, and were sometimes infilled with a slightly more prominent C peak internally.
evidence: This is a finding from VPSEM and EDS analysis, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Vessels in Centrosaurus bone occurred alongside white quartz crystals and smaller reddish minerals with high-Si content and Ba present.
source: Vessels occurred alongside white quartz crystals, which had strong Si peaks and overall were elementally similar to the vessels, and smaller reddish minerals, originally presumed to be iron oxide or pyrite, but which had high-Si content with Ba also present.
evidence: This is a finding from VPSEM and EDS analysis.

claim: Demineralization products of chicken bone and Pleistocene-Holocene shark tooth were much more homogenous and consisted of large fibrous masses.
source: Demineralization products differed from those of chicken bone (Figure 1C,G,M) and Pleistocene-Holocene shark tooth (Figure 1B,F,L), which were much more homogenous and consisted of large fibrous masses.
evidence: This is a comparative finding from microscopy, with reference to Figure 1.

claim: Chicken bone and shark tooth demineralization products were enriched in C, O, N, and S.
source: These more recent samples were enriched in C, O, N, and S, but the shark tooth also had a strong Fe signature and a relatively more prominent S peak than the chicken bone.
evidence: This is a finding from EDS analysis.

claim: The shark tooth had a strong Fe signature and a relatively more prominent S peak than the chicken bone.
source: These more recent samples were enriched in C, O, N, and S, but the shark tooth also had a strong Fe signature and a relatively more prominent S peak than the chicken bone.
evidence: This is a finding from EDS analysis.

claim: The chicken demineralisation product was white, while that of the shark tooth was black.
source: The chicken demineralisation product was white, while that of the shark tooth was black.
evidence: This is an observation from visual inspection.

claim: The dinosaur bone yielded different structures when the bone apatite was removed compared to the more recent bone.
source: These results show that the dinosaur bone yielded different structures when the bone apatite was removed compared to the more recent bone (i.e. primarily vessels as opposed to large fibrous masses).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the microscopy results.

claim: The dinosaur vessels are relatively inorganic in composition compared to the more recent bone, consistent with a mineralized biofilm.
source: Furthermore, the dinosaur vessels are relatively inorganic in composition compared to the more recent bone, consistent with a mineralized biofilm (Schultze-Lam et al., 1996; Decho, 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EDS results, supported by citations.

claim: ATR FTIR of a HCl demineralized vessel from subterranean Centrosaurus bone revealed somewhat poorly resolved, broad organic peaks.
source: ATR FTIR of a HCl demineralized, freeze-dried vessel from subterranean Centrosaurus bone revealed somewhat poorly resolved, broad organic peaks (Figure 2C) that were close in position to peaks that might be expected from various CH, CO, and amide bonds, as well as water, phosphate, and potentially carbonate and silicate bonds (Lindgren et al., 2011; Surmik et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017); also see publicly available NIST libraries).
evidence: This is a finding from ATR FTIR analysis, with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The ATR FTIR peaks in the dinosaur bone demineralization products could be consistent with various organic bonds present in more recent bone demineralization products.
source: These results show how, although potentially poorly resolved, the ATR FTIR peaks in the dinosaur bone demineralization products could be consistent with various organic bonds present in more recent bone demineralization products.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ATR FTIR results.

claim: The organic bonds detected by ATR FTIR are not necessarily ancient, endogenous, or protein-derived.
source: However, note that these bonds are relatively simple and could therefore be present in various organic molecules. Furthermore, they are not necessarily ancient, endogenous, or protein-derived.
evidence: This is a cautionary interpretation of the ATR FTIR results.

claim: Centrosaurus bone had a low pyrolysate yield as evidenced by significant column bleed at the end of the run.
source: Centrosaurus bone had a low pyrolysate yield (Figure 3B) as evidenced by the significant column bleed at the end of the run and contained mostly early eluting compounds.
evidence: This is a finding from Py-GC-MS analysis, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The pyrogram for Centrosaurus bone does not match that of modern collagen-containing bone.
source: The pyrogram for Centrosaurus bone does not match that of modern collagen-containing bone (Figure 3A), which contained many clear protein pyrolysis products such as nitriles and amides, and was most similar to mudstone matrix (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from Py-GC-MS analysis, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: The pyrogram for Centrosaurus bone was most similar to mudstone matrix.
source: The pyrogram for Centrosaurus bone does not match that of modern collagen-containing bone (Figure 3A), which contained many clear protein pyrolysis products such as nitriles and amides, and was most similar to mudstone matrix (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from Py-GC-MS analysis, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Subterranean Centrosaurus bone pyrolysates included alkylated benzenes and some polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons.
source: Subterranean Centrosaurus bone pyrolysates included alkylated benzenes and some polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (e.g. naphthalenes and fluorenes), and these can also be detected in the surrounding mudstone matrix (Figure 3C) and humic acid standard (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from Py-GC-MS analysis, with reference to Figure 3.

claim: Weak n-alkane/n-alkene doublets were possibly detected in the Late Cretaceous bones.
source: Weak n-alkane/n-alkene doublets were possibly detected in the Late Cretaceous bones (Figure 4A–D), and such doublets were also observed in the surrounding mudstone matrix (Figure 3C) and humic acid standard (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a finding from Py-GC-MS analysis, with reference to Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The dinosaur bone lacked any clear pyrolysis products indicative of high levels of protein preservation.
source: These results show how the dinosaur bone lacked any clear pyrolysis products indicative of high levels of protein preservation and instead had a chemical composition that more closely resembles potential environmental sources (i.e. mudstone matrix or humic acids) than bone proteins.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Py-GC-MS results.

claim: The dinosaur bone had a chemical composition that more closely resembles potential environmental sources than bone proteins.
source: These results show how the dinosaur bone lacked any clear pyrolysis products indicative of high levels of protein preservation and instead had a chemical composition that more closely resembles potential environmental sources (i.e. mudstone matrix or humic acids) than bone proteins.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Py-GC-MS results.

claim: Homologous series of n-alkane/n-alkene doublets may signify the presence of a kerogen-like substance in the dinosaur bone.
source: Homologous series of n-alkane/n-alkene doublets may signify the presence of a kerogen-like substance which could potentially be an ancient lipid-derived geopolymer in the dinosaur bone.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the Py-GC-MS results.

claim: Matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone had a total hydrolysable amino acid compositional profile that did not match collagen.
source: Matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone had a total hydrolysable amino acid (THAA) compositional profile that did not match collagen (Figure 6A,F).
evidence: This is a finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: Matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone appeared to be dominated by Gly, with Tyr also prominent, while being highly depleted in all the other amino acids.
source: The matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone appeared to be dominated by Gly, with Tyr also prominent, while being highly depleted in all the other amino acids.
evidence: This is a finding from HPLC amino acid analysis.

claim: Surface-eroded Late Cretaceous bone showed a different THAA composition to the matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone.
source: Surface-eroded Late Cretaceous bone from the same outcrop showed a different THAA composition to the matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone, even when examining bone eroded out of the BB180 quarry itself (Figure 6B,F).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: The uncovered subterranean Centrosaurus bone did not match the matrix-surrounded subterranean bone and was similar to the surface-eroded Late Cretaceous bone in THAA composition.
source: Furthermore, the uncovered subterranean Centrosaurus bone did not match the matrix-surrounded subterranean bone and was similar to the surface-eroded Late Cretaceous bone in THAA composition.
evidence: This is a comparative finding from HPLC amino acid analysis.

claim: Exposure to the surface changes the amino acid profile within Cretaceous fossils.
source: These results suggest that not only did the subterranean dinosaur bone not have an amino acid composition similar to collagen (i.e. Gallus and reference bone), but also that exposure to the surface changes the amino acid profile within these Cretaceous fossils.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HPLC amino acid analysis results.

claim: Subterranean Centrosaurus bone had a far lower THAA concentration than modern chicken bone.
source: Subterranean Centrosaurus bone had a far lower THAA concentration (summed total of all amino acids measured) than did the modern chicken bone (Figure 7A), as would be expected, and the uncovered subterranean Centrosaurus bone showed a higher THAA concentration than the matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: The uncovered subterranean Centrosaurus bone showed a higher THAA concentration than the matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone.
source: Subterranean Centrosaurus bone had a far lower THAA concentration (summed total of all amino acids measured) than did the modern chicken bone (Figure 7A), as would be expected, and the uncovered subterranean Centrosaurus bone showed a higher THAA concentration than the matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: Late Cretaceous bone tended to be L-amino acid dominated when amino acids were above detection limit.
source: Late Cretaceous bone tended to be L-amino acid dominated when amino acids were above detection limit (Table 1).
evidence: This is a finding from amino acid racemization analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claim: Low levels of racemization suggest that the amino acids in the dinosaur bone are not particularly ancient.
source: These low levels of racemization suggest that the amino acids in the dinosaur bone are not particularly ancient.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the racemization data.

claim: The adjacent mudstone matrix did not match the subterranean Centrosaurus bone in THAA compositional profile.
source: The adjacent mudstone matrix did not match the subterranean Centrosaurus bone in THAA compositional profile (Figure 6D,F).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: Surface-eroded Late Cretaceous bone showed some degree of similarity to topsoil in THAA composition.
source: Surface-eroded Late Cretaceous bone showed some degree of similarity to topsoil in THAA composition (Figure 6E,F), as did the various mudstone samples.
evidence: This is a comparative finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figure 6.

claim: Matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone showed the most different THAA compositional profile within the study.
source: Matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone showed the most different THAA compositional profile within the study (i.e. greatest separation from other data points in PC space).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the PCA results.

claim: The greatest variation between the samples was in relative Gly and Tyr concentrations.
source: The greatest variation between the samples of this study was in relative Gly and Tyr concentrations, with the matrix-surrounded subterranean Centrosaurus bone tending to have notably higher Gly and Tyr than collagen.
evidence: This is a finding from HPLC amino acid analysis.

claim: Subterranean dinosaur bone had a different amino acid composition than the surrounding mudstone.
source: These results suggest that subterranean dinosaur bone had a different amino acid composition than the surrounding mudstone and that the amino acid composition changes upon surface exposure, approaching that of topsoil.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HPLC amino acid analysis results.

claim: The amino acid composition of dinosaur bone changes upon surface exposure, approaching that of topsoil.
source: These results suggest that subterranean dinosaur bone had a different amino acid composition than the surrounding mudstone and that the amino acid composition changes upon surface exposure, approaching that of topsoil.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the HPLC amino acid analysis results.

claim: Topsoil showed a greater THAA concentration than subterranean and surface-eroded Centrosaurus bones, but not as high as modern chicken bones.
source: Topsoil showed a greater THAA concentration than subterranean and surface-eroded Centrosaurus bones, but not as high as modern chicken bones (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: Mudstone tended to have a very low THAA concentration, even compared to some of the Late Cretaceous bone samples.
source: Mudstone tended to have a very low THAA concentration, even compared to some of the Late Cretaceous bone samples (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is a finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figure 7.

claim: Topsoil contained a high amino acid concentration with relatively high rates of protein degradation, indicative of active biological accumulation and recycling.
source: These results show that topsoil contained a high amino acid concentration with relatively high rates of protein degradation, indicative of active biological accumulation and recycling, while mudstone contained low concentrations with very recent amino acids, indicative of low residence times of proteins within the mudstone.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid concentration and racemization data.

claim: Mudstone contained low amino acid concentrations with very recent amino acids, indicative of low residence times of proteins within the mudstone.
source: These results show that topsoil contained a high amino acid concentration with relatively high rates of protein degradation, indicative of active biological accumulation and recycling, while mudstone contained low concentrations with very recent amino acids, indicative of low residence times of proteins within the mudstone.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid concentration and racemization data.

claim: Fossil bones appeared to show instances of relatively greater accumulation of amino acids than the mudstone but with very recent amino acids.
source: The fossil bones appeared to show instances of relatively greater accumulation of amino acids than the mudstone but with very recent amino acids, indicative of preferential localization of biologically active amino acids to the bone compared to the mudstone, but with less amino acid content than topsoil.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid concentration and racemization data.

claim: Pleistocene-Holocene surface-eroded shark teeth had THAA compositional profiles that closely matched collagen.
source: Pleistocene-Holocene surface-eroded shark teeth had THAA compositional profiles that closely matched collagen (Figure 6A,C,F) and fairly high amino acid concentration with THAA concentrations between those of subterranean Centrosaurus bone and modern chicken bone (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a finding from HPLC amino acid analysis, with reference to Figures 6 and 7.

claim: Pleistocene-Holocene surface-eroded shark teeth had consistently high racemization, even more so than the topsoil sample.
source: Pleistocene-Holocene surface-eroded shark teeth, unlike the Late Cretaceous bone and mudstone, had consistently high racemization (Table 1), even more so than the topsoil sample.
evidence: This is a finding from amino acid racemization analysis, with reference to Table 1.

claim: The Pleistocene-Holocene teeth contained detectable, ancient amino acids consistent with endogenous collagen.
source: These results suggest that the Pleistocene-Holocene teeth contained detectable, ancient amino acids consistent with endogenous collagen.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid analysis results.

claim: Total organic carbon content was higher in the subterranean and surface-eroded Centrosaurus bone than the matrix.
source: Total organic carbon (TOC) content was higher in the subterranean and surface-eroded Centrosaurus bone than the matrix, even the directly adjacent matrix, and was comparable to that found in the topsoil (Table 2).
evidence: This is a finding from radiocarbon AMS analysis, with reference to Table 2.

claim: The organic carbon content in the Centrosaurus bones was significantly lower than the 82–71 ka Yarnton bovine bone sample known to contain well-preserved collagen.
source: However, the organic carbon content in the Centrosaurus bones was significantly lower than the 82–71 ka Yarnton bovine bone sample known to contain well-preserved (radiocarbon-dead) collagen (Cook et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a comparative finding from radiocarbon AMS analysis, with citation.

claim: TOC in the Centrosaurus bone was not found to be radiocarbon dead.
source: TOC in the Centrosaurus bone was not found to be radiocarbon dead, but did exhibit lower F14C values than both the mudstone and especially the topsoil.
evidence: This is a finding from radiocarbon AMS analysis.

claim: Approximately 26% of the C in subterranean Centrosaurus bone originates in the adjacent mudstone matrix, based on a simple two-end-member mixing model.
source: Assuming all endogenous bone C is radiocarbon 'dead', based on these F14C values, a simple two-end-member mixing model would suggest that ~26% of the C in subterranean Centrosaurus bone originates in the adjacent mudstone matrix (for formula, see Appendix 1 under the section entitled Carbon analysis).
evidence: This is a calculation based on radiocarbon data.

claim: The fossil dinosaur bone yielded a TOC content similar to relatively rich environmental carbon sources, such as topsoil.
source: The fossil dinosaur bone therefore yielded a TOC content similar to relatively rich environmental carbon sources, such as topsoil, but not as high as more recent bone proteins.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the radiocarbon data.

claim: Some of the C in the fossil dinosaur bone is potentially ancient, but there is still a sizable contribution of recent C from the immediate environment.
source: Although, some of the C in the fossil dinosaur bone is potentially ancient, there is still a sizable contribution of recent C from the immediate environment, consistent with the presence of a microbiome.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the radiocarbon data.

claim: DNA concentration was about 50 times higher in subterranean Centrosaurus bone than in adjacent mudstone matrix.
source: DNA concentration was about 50 times higher in subterranean Centrosaurus bone than in adjacent mudstone matrix (Table 3; Appendix 1—table 25).
evidence: This is a finding from DNA extraction and quantification, with reference to Table 3.

claim: PI staining for DNA on EDTA demineralized Centrosaurus bone revealed multi-cell aggregates forming organic vessel and fibrous conglomerate structures that fluoresce red.
source: PI staining for DNA on EDTA demineralized Centrosaurus bone revealed multi-cell aggregates forming organic vessel and fibrous conglomerate structures that fluoresce red (Figure 8A–D).
evidence: This is a finding from fluorescence microscopy, with reference to Figure 8.

claim: The DNA concentration in the bone indicates a cell concentration of ~4×10^8 cells/g.
source: The DNA concentration in the bone indicates a cell concentration of ~4×108 cells/g (calculation of cell abundance from DNA based on that of Magnabosco et al., 2018; also see Appendix 1—table 26).
evidence: This is a calculation based on DNA concentration data.

claim: The observed THAA concentration indicates ~3×10^8 cells/g in the bone.
source: This is fairly similar to the observed THAA concentration indicating ~3×108 cells/g (calculation of cell abundance from total amino acids based on that of Onstott et al., 2014 and Lomstein et al., 2012), consistent with the idea that the amino acids within the bone are likely to be largely cellular (i.e. lipid-bound within living organisms) due to the discrepancy between DNA and amino acid stability over time.
evidence: This is a calculation based on amino acid concentration data.

claim: The amino acids within the bone are likely to be largely cellular due to the discrepancy between DNA and amino acid stability over time.
source: This is fairly similar to the observed THAA concentration indicating ~3×108 cells/g (calculation of cell abundance from total amino acids based on that of Onstott et al., 2014 and Lomstein et al., 2012), consistent with the idea that the amino acids within the bone are likely to be largely cellular (i.e. lipid-bound within living organisms) due to the discrepancy between DNA and amino acid stability over time.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparing DNA and amino acid concentrations.

claim: The DNA concentration in the adjacent mudstone matrix indicates a cell concentration of ~5×10^6 cells/g.
source: The DNA concentration in the adjacent mudstone matrix indicate a cell concentration of ~5×106 cells/g, but the observed THAA concentration is consistent with a cell concentration of ~2×109 cells/g.
evidence: This is a calculation based on DNA concentration data.

claim: The subterranean dinosaur bone was enriched in cell-bound DNA relative to the mudstone matrix.
source: These results suggest that the subterranean dinosaur bone was enriched in cell-bound DNA relative to the mudstone matrix.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DNA concentration data.

claim: EDTA-extracted structures appeared to contain DNA from cells that aggregate within these structures, consistent with a modern biofilm.
source: Furthermore, EDTA-extracted structures appeared to contain DNA from cells that aggregate within these structures, consistent with a modern biofilm; the DNA itself had possibly been exposed due to the EDTA treatment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fluorescence microscopy results.

claim: 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing revealed the predominance of Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria in subterranean Centrosaurus bone.
source: The 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing revealed the predominance of Actinobacteria and Proteobacteria in subterranean Centrosaurus bone.
evidence: This is a finding from 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing.

claim: Sequences affiliated with classes Nitriliruptoria and Deltaproteobacteria were more abundant in bone relative to adjacent mudstone or the surface scrapings from the bone itself.
source: Sequences affiliated with classes Nitriliruptoria and Deltaproteobacteria were more abundant relative to adjacent mudstone or even the surface scrapings from the bone itself (Figure 9).
evidence: This is a finding from 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing, with reference to Figure 9.

claim: The majority of the sequences within Deltaproteobacteria were identified as belonging to the family Desulfurellaceae.
source: The majority of the sequences within Deltaproteobacteria were identified as belonging to the family Desulfurellaceae, which contains some sulfur-respiring species.
evidence: This is a finding from 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing.

claim: In Centrosaurus bone, about 30% of sequences were phylogenetically close to the genus Euzebya.
source: In Centrosaurus bone, about 30% of sequences were phylogenetically close to the genus Euzebya, a deeply branching, aerobic, marine Actinobacterium (Appendix 1—figure 58).
evidence: This is a finding from 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing.

claim: PCA shows that the differences between the interior bone cores and the mudstone or bone surface scrapings is greater than the difference between the mudstone and bone surface scrapings.
source: Furthermore, PCA of the species-level percentage data from these eight samples shows that the differences between the interior bone cores and the mudstone or bone surface scrapings is greater than the difference between the mudstone and bone surface scrapings (Appendix 1—figure 60).
evidence: This is a finding from PCA of 16S rRNA sequencing data.

claim: One-way PERMANOVA of species-level sequence percentages yielded significant differences between sample categories.
source: Likewise, one-way permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) performed in PAST3 software of species-level sequence percentages of the two replicates of each of the four sample categories in Figure 9 yielded significant differences (Euclidean similarity index; 9999 permutations; F = 53.16; p-value=0.0084), with greater similarity between the mudstone and bone surface scrapings than between either of these and the interior bone core samples (Appendix 1—table 27).
evidence: This is a statistical finding from analysis of 16S rRNA sequencing data.

claim: The subterranean dinosaur bone contained a different microbial community than the surrounding mudstone matrix.
source: These results suggest that the subterranean dinosaur bone contained a different microbial community than the surrounding mudstone matrix with some species potentially impacting fossil bone taphonomy and chemical composition.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the 16S rRNA sequencing results.

claim: Some microbes in the bone might represent rare, poorly understood taxa.
source: Our initial sequence data, furthermore, suggests that some of these microbes might represent rare, poorly understood taxa.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the 16S rRNA sequencing results.

claim: The occasional infilling observed in the HCl demineralized dinosaur bone vessels with greater C concentration in the interior is consistent with a growing biofilm.
source: The occasional infilling observed in the HCl demineralized dinosaur bone vessels with greater C concentration in the interior compared to the exterior of the vessel is consistent with a growing biofilm, given the assumption that a biofilm would grow inside the porous spaces of the bone while preserved vessels might be expected to be hollow.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EDS results.

claim: The Si dominance of the HCl demineralization products from the dinosaur bone likely suggests that they are at least partly silicified.
source: The Si dominance of the HCl demineralization products from the dinosaur bone likely suggest that they are at least partly silicified.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EDS results.

claim: HCl demineralization may favor mineralized biofilm retrieval.
source: HCl demineralization (especially the relatively intensive demineralization used on the samples that underwent microscopy, EDS, and ATR FTIR) may favor mineralized biofilm retrieval (assuming that low pH might degrade organically preserved biofilms), explaining why all the observed demineralization products of the dinosaur bone have high-Si content under EDS (especially in comparison to the presumably largely organic vessels and fibrous masses revealed using EDTA demineralization).
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the demineralization results.

claim: Any original organics in dinosaur bone are significantly more susceptible to acid than the organic masses in identically treated younger bone samples.
source: If this is the case then it would indicate that any original organics are significantly more susceptible to acid (i.e. of different composition) than the organic masses in the identically treated younger bone samples, which survive well.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential preservation of demineralization products.

claim: Mineral infilling in the Centrosaurus bone is largely of silicates, which have partly replaced the originally organic vessel-like structures.
source: It seems likely that mineral infilling in the Centrosaurus bone is largely of silicates, which have partly replaced the originally organic vessel-like structures, as well as, potentially, some barite or gypsum with minimal amounts of iron oxide or pyrite.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EDS results.

claim: Some inorganic compounds might contribute to the color of the fossils.
source: Some of these inorganic compounds might contribute to the color of the fossils.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: The fibrous material from HCl demineralization of the dinosaur bone may be silicified biofilm with a collagenous texture imprinted from the surrounding apatite matrix or may simply be a small misinterpreted quartz crystal.
source: The fibrous material from HCl demineralization of the dinosaur bone may be silicified biofilm with a collagenous texture imprinted from the surrounding apatite matrix or may simply be a small misinterpreted quartz crystal.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the microscopy results.

claim: A silicified biofilm might be a result of unique environmental conditions or microbial communities that these fossils experienced.
source: A silicified biofilm might be a result of unique environmental conditions (either early or late in the taphonomic history) or microbial communities that these fossils experienced.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: Examining fossils from different localities, climates, lithologies, and taphonomic histories is vital to understanding variation in how biofilms in fossil bone might be mineralized.
source: Therefore, examining fossils from different localities, climates, lithologies, and taphonomic histories is vital to understanding variation in how biofilms in fossil bone might be mineralized.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Humic acids are common in soils and contain low molecular weight, aromatic components.
source: Humic acids are common in soils and contain low molecular weight, aromatic components (Hatcher et al., 1981; Sutton and Sposito, 2005), and these were also detected in the humic acid standard, meaning that the early eluting, more volatile (i.e. lower boiling point), total ion chromatogram peaks from Py-GC/MS (e.g. the detected aromatic hydrocarbons) of the Centrosaurus bone may come from sources other than proteins.
evidence: This is supported by citations and is used to interpret the Py-GC-MS results.

claim: The early eluting peaks from Py-GC/MS of the Centrosaurus bone may come from sources other than proteins.
source: Humic acids are common in soils and contain low molecular weight, aromatic components (Hatcher et al., 1981; Sutton and Sposito, 2005), and these were also detected in the humic acid standard, meaning that the early eluting, more volatile (i.e. lower boiling point), total ion chromatogram peaks from Py-GC/MS (e.g. the detected aromatic hydrocarbons) of the Centrosaurus bone may come from sources other than proteins.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Py-GC-MS results.

claim: Py-GC/MS evidence of kerogen in the form of a homologous series of n-alkane/n-alkene doublets appears to have been detected in the Centrosaurus bone, but the doublets were very weak.
source: Py-GC/MS evidence of kerogen in the form of a homologous series of n-alkane/n-alkene doublets appears to have been detected in the Centrosaurus bone, but the doublets were very weak.
evidence: This is a finding from Py-GC-MS analysis.

claim: Variation in the visibility of the doublets between the matrix-surrounded and uncovered subterranean Centrosaurus bone samples is likely representative of intra-bone variation in kerogen content rather than contamination.
source: Variation in the visibility of the doublets between the matrix-surrounded and uncovered subterranean Centrosaurus bone samples is likely representative of intra-bone variation in kerogen content rather than contamination since a strong kerogen signature is not likely to result from exposure to air or the sterilized excavating equipment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the Py-GC-MS results.

claim: Kerogen forming from in situ polymerization of endogenous labile lipids might not be expected to preserve the tubular or hollow shape of 'soft tissues' with high fidelity.
source: Kerogen forming from in situ polymerization of endogenous labile lipids such as cell membranes might not be expected to preserve the tubular or hollow shape of 'soft tissues' such as vessels or cells in bone with high fidelity since initial hydrolytic cleavage from a hydrophilic group will eliminate the amphiphatic nature of these molecules and make them incapable of retaining their bilayer configuration in aqueous solution (Rand and Parsegian, 1989).
evidence: This is an inference based on lipid chemistry, supported by a citation.

claim: Cell membranes might lose their structure during kerogen formation, and the tubular or hollow structure of vessels or cells might be influenced as well.
source: Thus, cell membranes might lose their structure, and presumably, the tubular or hollow structure of vessels or cells might be influenced as well.
evidence: This is an inference based on lipid chemistry.

claim: The resulting kerogen could contribute to a non-tubular, low-resolution organic mold of 'soft tissues' formed in the cavities of the bone's inorganic matrix.
source: The possibility that the resulting kerogen could contribute to a non-tubular, low-resolution organic mold of such 'soft tissues' formed in the cavities of the bone's inorganic matrix should be considered in cases in which bone demineralization products are not mineralized.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation.

claim: EDS revealed prevalent mineralization of the structures studied, a common observation for such 'soft tissue' remains.
source: However, EDS revealed prevalent mineralization of the structures studied here, a common observation for such 'soft tissue' remains (Schweitzer et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from EDS analysis, with a citation to a previous study.

claim: Mineralization is more consistent with a biofilm origin rather than a kerogen origin.
source: This mineralization is more consistent with a biofilm origin (Schultze-Lam et al., 1996; Decho, 2010) rather than a kerogen origin.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EDS results, supported by citations.

claim: Kerogen-like aliphatic pyrolysis products have been detected using Py-GC-MS from the humic fraction of soil and the humic acid standard.
source: Furthermore, kerogen-like aliphatic pyrolysis products have previously been detected using Py-GC-MS from the humic fraction of soil as well as the humic acid standard, potentially derived from stable plant biopolymers from the cuticle (Saiz-Jimenez and De Leeuw, 1987), so kerogen-like material in the fossil bone could be derived, at least partly, from soil contaminants rather than being derived from endogenous lipids.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and is used to interpret the Py-GC-MS results.

claim: Kerogen-like material in the fossil bone could be derived, at least partly, from soil contaminants rather than being derived from endogenous lipids.
source: Furthermore, kerogen-like aliphatic pyrolysis products have previously been detected using Py-GC-MS from the humic fraction of soil as well as the humic acid standard, potentially derived from stable plant biopolymers from the cuticle (Saiz-Jimenez and De Leeuw, 1987), so kerogen-like material in the fossil bone could be derived, at least partly, from soil contaminants rather than being derived from endogenous lipids.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the Py-GC-MS results.

claim: The dominance of L-amino acids in the dinosaur fossils suggests significant leaching and degradation of endogenous amino acids, as well as relatively recent amino acid input.
source: The dominance of L-amino acids in the dinosaur fossils suggests significant leaching and degradation of endogenous amino acids, as well as relatively recent amino acid input.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid racemization data.

claim: There appears to be a trend toward greater concentration of amino acids in the dinosaur bone compared to the mudstone.
source: There appears to be a trend toward greater concentration of amino acids in the dinosaur bone compared to the mudstone, suggesting that the fossil bone might be preferentially concentrated in exogenous amino acids.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid concentration data.

claim: Cretaceous bone samples show evidence of bacterial contamination based on their Glx D/L values being greater than Asx D/L values.
source: Furthermore, Cretaceous bone samples, as in the uncovered subterranean Centrosaurus bone and the surface-eroded Late Cretaceous bone on the same ridge and ~21 m above BB180, show evidence of bacterial contamination. Their greater Glx D/L values than Asx D/L values are the reverse of that expected due to chemical racemization (Smith and Evans, 1980; Crisp et al., 2013), but in association with racemized Ala in these samples, they support the presence of peptidoglycans from bacterial cell walls, which contain D-amino acids, particularly D-Glu and D-Ala, in vivo (Höltje, 1998; Lam et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid racemization data, supported by citations.

claim: The observed dominance of gram-positive Actinobacteria in the Cretaceous bone microbiome is consistent with the presence of peptidoglycans.
source: This is consistent with the observed dominance of gram-positive Actinobacteria in the Cretaceous bone microbiome, since 26–75 wt% of the total cell dry weight of gram-positive bacteria comprises cell wall polymers and 7–56 wt% of the cellular amino acids comprises peptides from the cell wall peptidoglycan and teichoic acid and from S-layer glycoproteins (Onstott et al., 2014).
evidence: This is an interpretation linking amino acid and 16S rRNA sequencing data, supported by a citation.

claim: Differences in THAA compositions between surface-eroded and matrix-surrounded subterranean Late Cretaceous bone might suggest that subterranean bone provides a different microenvironment than surface-eroded bone.
source: The differences in THAA compositions between surface-eroded and matrix-surrounded subterranean Late Cretaceous bone might suggest that subterranean bone provides a different microenvironment than surface-eroded bone, perhaps largely driven by differences in oxygen availability, and thereby containing a different microbial community.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid composition data.

claim: Surface-eroded bone supports a microbial community more similar to other surface communities, such as topsoil.
source: This might suggest that surface-eroded bone supports a microbial community more similar to other surface communities, such as topsoil, while the subterranean bone contains a more different community.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid composition data.

claim: Variability in THAA concentration in the surface-eroded Late Cretaceous bones is not surprising given that one of the surface-eroded fragments appeared to have relatively higher mineral infiltration.
source: Variability in THAA concentration in the surface-eroded Late Cretaceous bones is not surprising given that one of the surface-eroded fragments appeared to have relatively higher mineral infiltration (evidenced by greater difficulty in powdering the sample), suggesting the potential for different microenvironments inside the bone and different carrying capacities for a microbial community.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid concentration data.

claim: The high THAA concentrations observed in one of the surface-eroded Late Cretaceous bones compared to the subterranean bone further suggests that bone can be colonized by exogenous microbes.
source: The high THAA concentrations observed in one of the surface-eroded Late Cretaceous bones compared to the subterranean bone further suggests that bone can be colonized by exogenous microbes, since surface exposure would be expected to result in adverse conditions for any surviving endogenous proteins.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid concentration data.

claim: Even relatively brief aerial exposure might lead to rapid contamination of the subterranean microbial community by surface microbes.
source: The most surprising result might be that the uncovered subterranean Centrosaurus bone sample had a THAA composition more closely matching surface-eroded bone than the matrix-surrounded subterranean bone, and also had an elevated THAA concentration compared to the matrix-surrounded subterranean bone, suggesting that even relatively brief aerial exposure might lead to rapid contamination of the subterranean microbial community by surface microbes.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid data.

claim: The high THAA concentration in the adjacent mudstone matrix of the subterranean bone compared to the other mudstone samples may indicate that bone provides a nutrient source that encourages microbial proliferation.
source: The high THAA concentration in the adjacent mudstone matrix of the subterranean bone compared to the other mudstone samples may indicate that bone provides a nutrient source that encourages microbial proliferation.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid concentration data.

claim: Lower F14C in the dinosaur bone compared to the mudstone or topsoil suggests some biologically inaccessible, old, and possibly endogenous C within the fossils.
source: However, lower F14C in the dinosaur bone compared to the mudstone or topsoil suggests some biologically inaccessible, old, and possibly endogenous C within the fossils.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the radiocarbon data.

claim: One possibility for the radiocarbon pattern is kerogen derived from in situ polymerization of endogenous dinosaur labile lipids.
source: One possibility for this pattern is kerogen derived from in situ polymerization of endogenous dinosaur labile lipids, although this type of aliphatic geopolymer has only been weakly detected in the Centrosaurus bones through Py-GC-MS (potentially due to methodology rather than low concentration), and it should be kept in mind that the surrounding mudstone matrix yields a series of n-alkanes/n-alkenes after pyrolysis.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the radiocarbon data.

claim: Exogenous C could become metabolically inaccessible in bone through biofilm mineralization.
source: Exogenous C could also become metabolically inaccessible in bone through biofilm mineralization, as suggested by the EDS data, allowing for 14C depletion.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the radiocarbon data.

claim: Biofilm formation and proliferation in bones could trap mobile organic C from sediment and groundwater at a rate faster than C exits the bone when not colonized by a biofilm.
source: Additionally, biofilm formation and proliferation in bones could trap mobile organic C from sediment and groundwater at a rate faster than C exits the bone when not colonized by a biofilm. This would allow for a lower F14C steady state to be reached during the time it takes C outflux to increase in order to match C influx, assuming a simple 1-box model.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the radiocarbon data.

claim: The microbial community from the EDTA demineralized bone was similar to that of the non-demineralized bone.
source: The microbial community from the EDTA demineralized bone was similar to that of the non-demineralized bone, important since EDTA can be used as the demineralizing agent to study the 'soft tissues' of fossil bone (Cleland et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from comparing 16S rRNA sequencing results, with a citation.

claim: Bone samples treated with common methods of demineralization in other taphonomic studies are amenable for nucleic acid analyses.
source: Thus, bone samples treated with common methods of demineralization in other taphonomic studies (e.g. antibody-based studies) are also amenable for nucleic acid analyses that can be used to help test the endogeneity of organics (i.e. whether there are microbes present that could possibly explain the presence of specific organics).
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity of microbial communities in demineralized and non-demineralized bone.

claim: PI staining of soft tissues is very likely due to cell rupture from exposure to the high concentrations of EDTA used during demineralization.
source: PI staining of soft tissues is very likely due to cell rupture from exposure to the high concentrations of EDTA used during demineralization (i.e. non-intact cells).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fluorescence microscopy results.

claim: The dominance of the aerobic Euzebya is consistent with the shallow depth of burial.
source: The dominance of the aerobic Euzebya is consistent with the shallow depth of burial, although the presence of the Deltaproteobacteria lineages may indicate that the microenvironment inside the fossil bone creates anaerobic niches to support anaerobic metabolism.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the 16S rRNA sequencing results.

claim: The presence of Deltaproteobacteria lineages may indicate that the microenvironment inside the fossil bone creates anaerobic niches to support anaerobic metabolism.
source: The dominance of the aerobic Euzebya is consistent with the shallow depth of burial, although the presence of the Deltaproteobacteria lineages may indicate that the microenvironment inside the fossil bone creates anaerobic niches to support anaerobic metabolism.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the 16S rRNA sequencing results.

claim: The fact that Actinobacteria were the most common microbes in the dinosaur bone is reminiscent of the results from a 38 ka Neanderthal bone.
source: The fact that Actinobacteria were the most common microbes in the dinosaur bone based on 16S rRNA amplicon sequencing is reminiscent of the results from a 38 ka Neanderthal bone, where the majority of detected DNA sequences derived from non-ancient Actinobacteria (Zaremba-Niedźwiedzka and Andersson, 2013).
evidence: This is a comparative observation supported by a citation.

claim: The high cell concentrations of ~5×10^8 cells/g in the subterranean Centrosaurus bone indicates a microbial community that is more substantial than that of the adjacent mudstone.
source: The high cell concentrations of ~5×108 cells/g in the subterranean Centrosaurus bone and the consistency in the DNA and amino-acid-based estimates indicates a microbial community that is more substantial than that of the adjacent mudstone.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the DNA and amino acid concentration data.

claim: HCl demineralization products of dinosaur fossil bone differ structurally and elementally from the Pleistocene-Holocene and modern samples.
source: HCl demineralization products of dinosaur fossil bone differ structurally and elementally from the Pleistocene-Holocene and modern samples when examined using light microscopy and VPSEM.
evidence: This is a summary of the microscopy and EDS findings.

claim: The Pleistocene-Holocene shark tooth and modern chicken bone demineralize to reveal large organic masses consistent with collagen protein.
source: The Pleistocene-Holocene shark tooth and modern chicken bone demineralize to reveal large organic masses (i.e. rich in C and O) consistent with collagen protein as evidenced by discernable N and S peaks, unlike the much older dinosaur bone demineralization products.
evidence: This is a summary of the microscopy and EDS findings.

claim: The relatively more pronounced S peak in the shark tooth might indicate sulfurization of the collagen protein or some other taphonomic incorporation of inorganic S from the environment into the tooth.
source: The relatively more pronounced S peak in the shark tooth as compared to the chicken bone might indicate sulfurization of the collagen protein or some other taphonomic incorporation of inorganic S from the environment into the tooth, the latter being consistent with pyrite.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the EDS results.

claim: The high Fe content in the shark tooth suggests some taphonomic mineral accumulation and may explain some of the dark discoloration in the teeth.
source: The high Fe content in the shark tooth suggests some taphonomic mineral accumulation (e.g. iron oxide or pyrite) and may explain some of the dark discoloration in the teeth, potentially alongside a browning effect caused by the taphonomic formation of melanoidin-like N-heterocyclic polymers known as advanced glycoxidation/lipoxidation end products.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the EDS results.

claim: Raman spectroscopy has been used to suggest that N-heterocyclic polymers are present in ancient teeth, bone, and eggshell, and that they lead to brown staining.
source: Raman spectroscopy has not only been used to suggest that these N-heterocyclic polymers are present in ancient teeth, bone, and eggshell, but also that they lead to brown staining (Wiemann et al., 2018b).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Wiemann et al., 2018b.

claim: Given the open system behavior of bone, detected polymers could derive from exogenous sources of polypeptides and lipids/polysaccharides.
source: However, it should be kept in mind that, given the open system behavior of bone, detected polymers could derive from exogenous sources of polypeptides and lipids/polysaccharides (e.g. either ancient or more recent infiltrating microbes), and the presence of any amide bands in Raman spectra is likely insufficient evidence for endogenous oligopeptide preservation (see a similar discussion of amide bands in FTIR below) especially in association with polymers that form as a result of protein degradation (Singh et al., 2001; Vistoli et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a cautionary interpretation supported by citations.

claim: Similar FTIR peaks to those detected here are used as evidence for purported dinosaur collagen, but such results are not conclusive of collagen.
source: Similar, albeit higher resolution, FTIR peaks to those detected here are used as evidence for purported dinosaur collagen (Lindgren et al., 2011; Surmik et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017), but, it should be noted that such results are not conclusive of collagen.
evidence: This is a critical interpretation of the use of FTIR in other studies, supported by citations.

claim: Detection of peaks associated with amide bonds may not necessarily indicate intact proteins/peptides, since amide bonds are not specific to peptides.
source: Detection of peaks such as those associated with amide bonds may not necessarily indicate intact proteins/peptides, since amide bonds are not specific to peptides and can be found in protein degradation products such as diketopiperazines (Chiavari and Galletti, 1992; Martins and Carvalho, 2007; Saitta et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is a cautionary interpretation supported by citations.

claim: CH and CO bonds are widely distributed, found in a variety of organic molecules.
source: CH and CO bonds are even more widely distributed, found in a variety of organic molecules.
evidence: This is a statement about chemical knowledge.

claim: Without deconvolution of peaks to produce fingerprints of protein secondary structure, one cannot say from the presence of organic bonds alone that the protein is collagen, let alone endogenous or ancient.
source: Even if such bonds are from proteins, without deconvolution of peaks to produce fingerprints of protein secondary structure (Byler and Susi, 1986), one cannot say from the presence of such organic bonds alone that the protein is collagen, let alone endogenous or ancient.
evidence: This is a critical interpretation of FTIR methodology, supported by a citation.

claim: Variation in the phosphate bands derived from ATR FTIR of bone can be affected by bone collagen content.
source: It has been shown experimentally and theoretically that variation in the phosphate bands derived from ATR FTIR of bone can be affected by bone collagen content, with low-frequency symmetry of the phosphate peaks more apparent in bone containing lower amounts of collagen (Aufort et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Aufort et al., 2018.

claim: The observation of sharper, more symmetric phosphate peaks in the Centrosaurus bone compared to the younger bone might suggest lower relative collagen content.
source: The observation of sharper, more symmetric phosphate peaks in the Centrosaurus bone compared to the younger bone might suggest lower relative collagen content.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the ATR FTIR results.

claim: The presence of protein-related pyrolysis products does not indicate that these proteins are necessarily ancient, endogenous, or collagenous.
source: Regardless, the presence of protein-related pyrolysis products does not indicate that these proteins are necessarily ancient, endogenous, or collagenous.
evidence: This is a cautionary interpretation of the Py-GC-MS results.

claim: Amino acids in the dinosaur bone are dominated by proteins other than collagen and appear to be relatively recent.
source: Amino acids in the dinosaur bone are dominated by proteins other than collagen and appear to be relatively recent.
evidence: This is a summary of the amino acid analysis findings.

claim: Low amino acid concentrations, low D-amino acid concentrations, and THAA compositional profiles that do not match collagen suggest that the majority of the endogenous collagen protein has been lost from the dinosaur fossils.
source: Low amino acid concentrations, low D-amino acid concentrations, and THAA compositional profiles that do not match collagen, despite high Gly content, suggest that the majority of the endogenous collagen protein has been lost from the dinosaur fossils.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid analysis results.

claim: Changes in the THAA compositional profile as a result of taphonomic alteration and preferential loss of less stable amino acids would be expected in samples of this age.
source: Changes in the THAA compositional profile as a result of taphonomic alteration and preferential loss of less stable amino acids would be expected in samples of this age, with any remaining endogenous protein likely to have low levels of sequence and higher order structural preservation, with a consequent impact on the preservation of epitopes for antibodies.
evidence: This is an inference based on taphonomic expectations.

claim: The much younger shark teeth from the Pleistocene-Holocene have relatively high amino acid concentrations whose THAA compositional profiles are consistent with a dominance of collagen.
source: In contrast to the Late Cretaceous bone, the much younger shark teeth from the Pleistocene-Holocene have relatively high amino acid concentrations whose THAA compositional profiles are consistent with a dominance of collagen.
evidence: This is a summary of the amino acid analysis findings.

claim: Ethanol rinsing did not change the THAA compositional profile of shark teeth, suggesting that the majority of the organics are deriving from insoluble collagen with fairly well preserved higher order structure.
source: Since ethanol rinsing did not change the THAA compositional profile of shark teeth, this suggests that the majority of the organics are deriving from insoluble collagen with fairly well preserved higher order structure, rather than highly fragmented peptides with greater mobility.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid analysis results.

claim: The shark teeth have relatively high racemization, a testament to the antiquity of the amino acids as would be expected from endogenous proteins.
source: The shark teeth also have relatively high racemization, a testament to the antiquity of the amino acids as would be expected from endogenous proteins.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the amino acid racemization data.

claim: Previous studies have often reported purported endogenous 'soft tissues' within fossil dinosaur bone, but these studies often do not fully address fossil bones being open systems that are biologically active.
source: Previous studies have often reported purported endogenous 'soft tissues' within fossil dinosaur bone (Pawlicki et al., 1966; Schweitzer et al., 2005a; Schweitzer et al., 2005b; Schweitzer et al., 2007a; Schweitzer et al., 2007b; Schweitzer et al., 2008; Schweitzer et al., 2009; Schweitzer et al., 2013; Schweitzer et al., 2014; Schweitzer et al., 2016; Asara et al., 2007; Organ et al., 2008; Schweitzer, 2011; Bertazzo et al., 2015; Cleland et al., 2015; Schroeter et al., 2017). However, these studies often do not fully address fossil bones being open systems that are biologically active.
evidence: This is a critical statement about previous research, supported by citations.

claim: Fossil bone is frequently colonized by lichen on the surface or overgrown and penetrated by plant roots in the subsurface.
source: This can be seen in field observations, in Dinosaur Provincial Park and elsewhere, where fossil bone is frequently colonized by lichen on the surface or overgrown and penetrated by plant roots in the subsurface.
evidence: This is based on field observations.

claim: Subsurface biota could contaminate bone.
source: This forces researchers to consider that subsurface biota (e.g. plant roots, fungi, animals, protists, and bacteria) could contaminate bone.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of biological activity around fossils.

claim: Fungi can produce collagen.
source: Given that fungi can produce collagen (Celerin et al., 1996), the need to rule out exogenous sources of organics in fossil bone is made all the greater.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Celerin et al., 1996.

claim: Deeply buried bone has the potential to be biologically active, given the high concentration of microorganisms in continental subsurface sedimentary rock.
source: Even deeply buried bone has the potential to be biologically active, given the high concentration of microorganisms in continental subsurface sedimentary rock (Magnabosco et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Magnabosco et al., 2018.

claim: The analyses presented here are consistent with the idea that far from being biologically 'dead', fossil bone supports a diverse, active, and specialized microbial community.
source: The analyses presented here are consistent with the idea that far from being biologically 'dead', fossil bone supports a diverse, active, and specialized microbial community.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: It is necessary to rule out the hypothesis of subsurface contamination before concluding that fossils preserve geochemically unstable endogenous organics, like proteins.
source: Given this, it is necessary to rule out the hypothesis of subsurface contamination before concluding that fossils preserve geochemically unstable endogenous organics, like proteins.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: We detected no evidence of endogenous proteins in the bone studied here.
source: We detected no evidence of endogenous proteins in the bone studied here and were therefore unable to replicate claims of protein survival from deep time, such as the Mesozoic (Pawlicki et al., 1966; Schweitzer et al., 2005a; Schweitzer et al., 2007a; Schweitzer et al., 2007b; Schweitzer et al., 2008; Schweitzer et al., 2009; Schweitzer et al., 2013; Schweitzer et al., 2014; Schweitzer et al., 2016; Asara et al., 2007; Organ et al., 2008; Schweitzer, 2011; Bertazzo et al., 2015; Cleland et al., 2015; Schroeter et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a primary conclusion of the study.

claim: Recent Pleistocene-Holocene material often shows clear, and multiple lines of, evidence for endogenous, ancient collagen.
source: In contrast, recent Pleistocene-Holocene material often shows clear, and multiple lines of, evidence for endogenous, ancient collagen.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from the Pleistocene-Holocene shark teeth.

claim: Detection of specific organic signatures in fossils requires corroborating evidence before claims of ancient proteins can be substantiated.
source: Detection of specific organic signatures in fossils (e.g. amide bands in FTIR or Raman spectroscopy) requires corroborating evidence before claims of ancient proteins can be substantiated.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Evidence is required to identify the type of protein, demonstrate its endogenous origin, and demonstrate its age.
source: In addition to reliable markers of general protein presence (e.g. amide, succinimide, or piperazine pyrolysis products), evidence is required to identify the type of protein (i.e. amino acid composition or sequence) as well demonstrate its endogenous origin (e.g. localization) and age (i.e. degree of degradation as revealed by amino acid racemization, post-translational modifications such as deamidation, or peptide length/degree of hydrolysis).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Degradation of collagen polypeptides follows a pattern of gradual hydrolysis at the terminal ends followed by catastrophic degradation and rapid hydrolysis due to rupture of the triple helix quaternary structure.
source: Degradation of collagen polypeptides follows a pattern of gradual hydrolysis of amino acids at the terminal ends followed by catastrophic degradation and rapid hydrolysis due to rupture of the triple helix quaternary structure, making the resulting gelatinous fragments susceptible to rapid leaching from the bone or microbial degradation (Collins et al., 1995; Collins et al., 2009; Dobberstein et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on collagen degradation.

claim: If ancient collagen does persist in a fossil bone, then such preservation would often provide clear, strong structural and chemical signatures like that in the Pleistocene-Holocene shark teeth.
source: It might therefore be suspected that if ancient collagen does indeed persist in a fossil bone, then such preservation would often provide clear, strong structural and chemical signatures like that in the Pleistocene-Holocene shark teeth.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings.

claim: Techniques that do not provide information on the precise sequence or post-translational modification of peptides have been suggested to be outdated for palaeoproteomic studies.
source: Recently it has been suggested that techniques that do not provide information on the precise sequence or post-translational modification of peptides, such as Py-GC-MS or HPLC amino acid analysis, are outdated for palaeoproteomic studies (Cleland and Schroeter, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cleland and Schroeter, 2018.

claim: Techniques like Py-GC-MS or HPLC should be considered frontline approaches when dealing with samples of significant age and/or thermal maturity.
source: However, our results here suggest that techniques like Py-GC-MS or HPLC that give more general information on protein presence versus absence or general amino acid composition should be considered frontline approaches when dealing with samples of significant age and/or thermal maturity (e.g. Demarchi et al., 2016; Hendy et al., 2018; Cappellini et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings, supported by citations.

claim: Treating Mesozoic bone that has experienced diagenesis, low latitudes, and permineralisation identically to more recent, less altered bone is ill-advised.
source: Treating Mesozoic bone that has experienced diagenesis, low latitudes, and permineralisation identically to more recent, less altered bone is ill-advised, and any work on such samples should employ these fundamental methods before attempting to sequence peptides that might not be present, ancient, or endogenous.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Fossil bone has fairly high concentrations of recent organics, even when buried and often in comparison to the immediate environment.
source: Fossil bone has fairly high concentrations of recent organics (e.g. L-amino acids, DNA, and non-radiocarbon dead organic C), even when buried and often in comparison to the immediate environment.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Fossil bone likely provides an ideal, nutrient-rich open system microbial habitat inside vascular canals capable of moisture retention.
source: Fossil bone likely provides an ideal, nutrient-rich (e.g. phosphate, iron) open system microbial habitat inside vascular canals capable of moisture retention.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the study's findings.

claim: The absence of evidence for endogenous proteins and the presence of a diverse, microbial community urge caution regarding claims of dinosaur bone 'soft tissues'.
source: The absence of evidence for endogenous proteins and the presence of a diverse, microbial community urge caution regarding claims of dinosaur bone 'soft tissues'.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Microbes can colonize bones while buried, likely traveling via groundwater.
source: Microbes can colonize bones while buried, likely traveling via groundwater.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings.

claim: It is unsurprising that the prevalence of 'soft tissues' is not correlated with overburden depth above the fossil or cortical versus cancellous bone tissue.
source: Therefore, it is unsurprising that the prevalence of these 'soft tissues' is not correlated with overburden depth above the fossil or cortical versus cancellous bone tissue (Ullmann et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings, supported by a citation.

claim: Minimum distance from the surface is probably of importance for microbial colonization.
source: Rather, minimum distance from the surface is probably of importance and microbes likely readily colonize a variety of bone tissue types since both presumably behave as open systems.
evidence: This is an inference based on the study's findings.

claim: Our results support the hypothesis that at least some 'soft tissue' structures derived from demineralised fossil bones represent biofilms.
source: Our results support the hypothesis that at least some 'soft tissue' structures derived from demineralised fossil bones represent biofilms.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: Unless in an inaccessible form or matrix, endogenous dinosaur organics that survive prior taphonomic processes may be subject to subsequent microbial metabolic recycling.
source: We suggest that unless in an inaccessible form (e.g. kerogen, depending on microbial metabolic ability) or matrix (e.g. well-cemented concretion), endogenous dinosaur organics that survive prior taphonomic processes (e.g. diagenesis) may be subject to subsequent microbial metabolic recycling.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.

claim: The study of fossil organics must consider potential microbial presence throughout a specimen's taphonomic history, from early to late.
source: The study of fossil organics must consider potential microbial presence throughout a specimen's taphonomic history, from early to late.
evidence: This is a recommendation based on the study's findings.

claim: Microbial communities interact with fossils immediately following death and after burial, but prior to diagenesis.
source: Microbial communities interact with fossils immediately following death and after burial, but prior to diagenesis.
evidence: This is a statement about taphonomic processes.

claim: Microbes are known to utilize bone and tooth proteins.
source: Microbes are known to utilize bone and tooth proteins (Child et al., 1993) and fossil evidence of early fungal colonization has even been detected (Owocki et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Child et al., 1993 and Owocki et al., 2016.

claim: More recent microbial colonization of fossil bone will occur as it nears the surface during uplift and erosion in the late stages of the taphonomic process.
source: More recent microbial colonization of fossil bone will occur as it nears the surface during uplift and erosion in the late stages of the taphonomic process.
evidence: This is an inference about taphonomic processes.

claim: Given that microbes can inhabit the crust kilometres below the surface, it might be predicted that bone remains a biologically active habitat even when buried hundreds of meters deep for millions of years.
source: Furthermore, given that microbes can inhabit the crust kilometres below the surface (Magnabosco et al., 2018), it might be predicted that bone remains a biologically active habitat even when buried hundreds of meters deep for millions of years.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of the deep biosphere, supported by a citation.

claim: The extensive potential for microbial contamination and metabolic consumption makes verifying claims of Mesozoic bone protein extremely challenging.
source: The extensive potential for microbial contamination and metabolic consumption makes verifying claims of Mesozoic bone protein extremely challenging.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the study's findings.
